In Magen Avraham, seif katan 6, the text should read: "It is not comparable to what is written in siman 585," etc.; if another performed the brit milah, that other person recites the blessing, and see Tur, siman 641. The intent appears to me as follows. Certainly, where the person obligated in the mitzvah performs the mitzvah himself, he can fulfill the blessing through another person, as explained in siman 8, seif katan 8, in the name of Hagahot Ashiri. Thus regarding shofar, the blower may properly recite the blessing, because the person obligated to hear the shofar hears it and thereby performs the mitzvah himself, while the blower discharges him with the blessing. What Magen Avraham calls "the hearer" means the person obligated to hear the shofar sound, who hears it from this blower, hears the blessing, and fulfills his obligation through it.

Here, however, the obligated person performs no act of mitzvah at all; another person performs the mitzvah. One might therefore say that the other person should not recite the blessing because the mitzvah is not incumbent upon him. This is unlike separating terumot and maaserot, where an appointed agent recites the blessing, as is implied regarding challah. There, the agent who separates is himself connected to the matter, because he too may not eat from the dough before separation. That consideration does not exist here.

Nevertheless, it is possible that if the homeowner is present at the time of the blessing, Magen Avraham agrees that the agent may properly recite the blessing. Since the homeowner, who is obligated to perform the search, fulfills his obligation through this agent, the agent is like him and it is as though the homeowner searched himself. The homeowner therefore bears an obligation to recite a blessing over this search and fulfills it through the blessing recited by the searching agent.

Magen Avraham, however, inferred from the wording "if the homeowner wishes," etc., that only in such a case do they rely upon the homeowner's intention; otherwise the searchers recite the blessing themselves. This is difficult. If the homeowner is present while the other person is about to search, it is obvious that it is preferable for the homeowner himself to recite the blessing and for the agent to search under the homeowner's blessing, since the homeowner is the obligated party. It must therefore mean that even if the homeowner does not wish to fulfill his blessing through the agent's blessing, the other person who searches nevertheless recites the blessing. Magen Avraham then asks why he should bless when the homeowner is not there to fulfill his obligation through this blessing and the agent himself has no obligation to search.

He answers that this resembles brit milah, where the other person who performs the act recites the blessing, apparently even if the father is absent, because the mohel is nevertheless performing a mitzvah. Here too, the searcher performs a mitzvah even though the mitzvah is not personally incumbent upon him.

This comparison is somewhat difficult, because brit milah is different. If the father does not perform the brit milah, beit din is obligated to do so. Thus the mitzvah is one in which the agent himself has a halachic connection. By contrast, if a homeowner refuses to search his own house, no obligation rests upon another person to search that homeowner's house. I found that Dagul Merevavah likewise leaves this requiring study.

Magen Avraham then writes: see Tur, siman 641. There it is explained that one who performs a mitzvah for others also recites the blessing. Magen Avraham cites these words of Tur also in siman 366, seif katan 20, and there also cites Rambam that one who affixes a mezuzah for others recites the blessing. He distinguishes a case in which the one reciting the blessing performs an act.

See Bach, siman 676, who writes in manuscript that where the mitzvah rests on the person's body, such as lighting Chanukah lights, one who lights for another does not recite the blessing, whereas where the object itself requires a mitzvah act, such as separating terumot and maaserot, the agent recites the blessing. This distinction can be understood according to Tosafos Rid in Kiddushin, who explains that agency does not work where one says to another, "Put on tefillin for me," or, "Sit in the sukkah for me," because the mitzvah rests upon the body of the person himself.

Accordingly, even with Chanukah lights, when another person lights for him, this is not an ordinary law of agency. Rather, the mitzvah incumbent upon the person is that a Chanukah light be kindled in his house, and there is no distinction whether he himself lights it or another person lights it. The person lighting merely effects the state required for the obligated person, comparable to telling another person to place tefillin upon him. Since the lighter does not have the status of an agent in the usual sense, he does not recite a blessing because the mitzvah is not incumbent upon him.

Where the mitzvah rests upon the object, however, such as separating terumot and maaserot, the appointed agent is legally like the homeowner and therefore properly recites the blessing. The essential distinction between an obligation resting on the person and one resting on the object is that an object-based obligation is not constant. If a person has no produce, or does not wish to eat it, there is no obligation upon him to separate terumah. Tefillin and Chanukah lights, however, are personal obligations that rest upon the individual.

Regarding bedikat chametz, it requires study whether it resembles Chanukah lights, because the mitzvah rests upon the individual to search his domain for chametz, and ordinarily every person has a place in which he keeps chametz during the year and the Sages enacted that it be searched on the 14th; yet another person's search for him works just as another person's lighting works for Chanukah, perhaps not through the law of agency. Or perhaps, since the essence of the mitzvah is that his domain be searched of chametz, it is an obligation upon the object, like separating terumah, and agency is fully effective. In any event, when the homeowner is standing there, either way the searching agent may properly recite the blessing. This is also explained in siman 670 in Bach's words cited by Magen Avraham.

Regarding brit milah, my grandfather, the Gaon and author of Tevuot Shor, siman 28, writes that we apply the rule that a person's agent is like himself. His words require some examination, but this is not the place.

As for the words, "And the custom is to place chametz nuksheh," this means hardened chametz and refers to Rama's statement, "And the custom is to place," etc. It is also possible that this is a separate reference marker upon Rama's words.

"That I did not see and did not destroy." Chametz that he did see and set aside for destruction is not nullified now, because he still intends to eat some of what he leaves over and also wishes to fulfill the mitzvah of burning his own chametz the following day. He therefore does not nullify everything until the next day, after eating and after burning the chametz.

"Let it be nullified and become." See Bach, who discusses at length the dispute among the Rishonim. According to Rabbeinu Chananel and those who agree with him, nullification functions as hefker. Responsa Maharik, siman 142, however, writes that according to Rashi, Rambam, and those who agree with them, it does not function as hefker, but as rendering the chametz like dust. Kol Bo writes likewise. Thus our formula, which does not explicitly say "hefker," relies upon Rashi and those who agree with him. Bach discusses the matter at length and holds that the primary view is Rabbeinu Tam, and therefore concludes that it is proper to say: "Any chametz in my possession that I did not see, did not destroy, and do not know about shall be nullified and become ownerless like the dust of the earth." The later authorities agree.

"Whether he understands it." This is the reading found in most books. Some books read: "If he said it in the Holy Tongue, he has fulfilled his obligation," meaning even if he does not understand it. Olat Shabbos writes likewise because it troubled those authors that the formula Kol Chamira is not literally Hebrew. My brother-in-law, however, in Eliyah Zuta, resolves the old text by explaining that the author calls the Talmudic language of Kol Chamira "the Holy Tongue." Shaar Ephraim in the addendum, page 113b, seeks to object that Kol Chamira is not Hebrew, but this is not an objection. Relative to ordinary vernaculars, the Talmudic language can be called the Holy Tongue. I found explicit support in Agudah, first chapter of Pesachim, siman 1. After recording the Kol Chamira formula, it writes that if one does not know how to say it in the Holy Tongue, he should say it in German or another language that he understands. This explicitly supports my brother-in-law's explanation of Rama.

"But in other languages he must mention each separately." The same applies if one uses literal Hebrew rather than the established Talmudic formula: he must mention both chametz and se'or, as explained in Beit Yosef. Ordinarily, however, everyone recites the formula established by the Sages. A person who changes from it generally does so because he is unlearned and does not understand the established formula or Hebrew, and therefore says it in the vernacular.

If he utters words in a language that he does not understand and has no awareness that he is nullifying his chametz, he certainly has not fulfilled the obligation. If, however, he knows that the statement is an act of nullification and intends to nullify his chametz, he fulfills the obligation even if he does not understand every individual word, because nullification in the heart is also effective. The later authorities agree. In this respect there is no distinction between Hebrew and another language.

(1) "In any amount," etc. Regarding a prohibited item that became prohibited through a mashehu and was then mixed into another cooked food, Taz discusses the matter at length in Yoreh De'ah, siman 92. He concludes: if a piece became prohibited through a mashehu and afterward fell into another mixture and was removed, what it exudes does not prohibit the second mixture through a mashehu. But when liquid became mixed with liquid in this way, it remains prohibited through a mashehu. End quote.

Nekudat HaKesef strongly disagrees and writes that this is astonishing, for the halachic decisors all prohibit it. In any event, he argues, the minute prohibited flavor within that piece, since it is mixed together with another substance, should be considered a different species relative to the other pieces, because the other pieces do not contain that mixture; and on Pesach even unlike species are forbidden through a mashehu.

In my humble opinion, the words of Taz are correct. Tosafos in Chullin explain the law of a piece becoming neveilah. Rabbeinu Ephraim holds that chatichah na'asit neveilah applies only to meat and milk. Accordingly, in other prohibitions the permitted material does not itself become like the prohibition. If the prohibited flavor does not impart taste into the piece, it does not have the power to spread outward from that piece. The same applies even according to Rabbeinu Tam, who holds that chatichah na'asit neveilah applies to other prohibitions as well: that stringency was said only where the prohibition imparts taste. Where it does not impart taste, such as where the piece contains 60 times the prohibition, the Sages did not say that the permitted portion becomes exactly like the prohibited portion. Accordingly, where the entire prohibition is only because of a mashehu, that mashehu does not have power to spread farther. This appears to me clear in Tosafos. The same is implied by Rashba's novellae, Mishmeret HaBayit, Sefer HaTerumah, and the Rosh.

Nekudat HaKesef relied upon Ran at the end of Perek Gid HaNasheh, who writes that although like species are not nullified, we do not find this where another permitted taste is mixed in. He understood this to mean that because another force is mixed in, it becomes unlike species. That is not correct. Ran's intent is that the additional permitted flavor weakens the identity of the original prohibited flavor for purposes of the rule of like species; it does not mean that every piece containing a trace becomes a new unlike species that can transmit a Pesach mashehu indefinitely.

Taz also cites a ruling concerning a wheat kernel found in cooked food and a spoon inserted afterward. Some understood from that case that once the kernel was removed, a spoon inserted into the food would not later prohibit another food through a mashehu. I wonder at that reasoning. If so, what do we do every day when a pot contains several pieces of meat and a dairy spoon is inserted, where everything in the pot is combined toward 60, as is explicit in many places? Let us be concerned that perhaps the spoon touched only 1 piece, which absorbed by itself without 60. Rather, certainly all the contents combine.

Therefore the answer is as I wrote in Eliyah Zuta: specifically from a food piece, a mashehu does not have power to spread further, because the piece has its own permitted flavor. A spoon, which has no independent flavor of its own, is different; what it absorbed can spread from it. Rama makes a similar distinction in Yoreh De'ah, siman 105, seif 7.

Nekudat HaKesef further challenges Taz: why did he specify that the prohibited piece fell into another mixture and was removed? Even if it was not removed, it should not prohibit the other pieces. He concludes that the wording is a scribal error. In my humble opinion, Taz's wording is correct. He means to exclude a case where the prohibited piece is no longer recognizable. In that case, since the piece itself remains prohibited, as Tosafos write, and on Pesach dry food is not nullified even in dry food, the entire mixture becomes prohibited. I proved this at length in Eliyah Zuta from Tosafos and the Rosh, although I also raised a question there concerning the Rosh in Avodah Zarah, Perek HaSocher; here I record only what is necessary for practical halacha.

Nekudat HaKesef also sought proof from siman 467, seif 12, where Rama writes that if it became mixed with other pieces one may be lenient because of doubt, which would imply that where the matter is certain the mixture is forbidden. Magen Avraham writes similarly there. This is not a proof. One can say that the case there is where the second cooked food does not contain a majority against the pieces. Alternatively, Rama may not be discussing the food piece at all, but rather a liquid mixture, regarding which we are lenient only because of a rabbinic doubt.

Furthermore, even if that were Rama's view, I have already proved from Tosafos and the great halachic decisors that the food piece is permitted in the manner explained above. Taz himself later reinforced his ruling in Orach Chayyim and wrote that it is a peg that cannot be moved. The practical conclusion is therefore to be lenient where a recognizable piece became prohibited through a mashehu and afterward fell into another cooked food that contains a majority against it, provided the prohibited piece is removed. If the piece is not recognizable, everything is forbidden. A spoon, however, that absorbed a mashehu can prohibit another mixture through a mashehu.
